title: Cover Story: Debt repayment looms for Genting
body:
This article first appeared in The Edge Malaysia Weekly on October 19, 2026 - October 25, 2026
A generation of investors grew up believing that Genting Bhd (KL:GENTING) was a cash-generating machine for which nothing could go wrong even during the worst of times.
It survived economic turmoil and the pandemic, and was favoured by mom-and-pop investors for its regular dividends.
For more than 50 years, the cash generated by Malaysia’s sole casino, located at the peak of Gunung Ulu Kali, was enough to keep shareholders happy while helping fuel the group’s global operations.
Majority-owned by the Lim family, the casino earned the moniker “one-hill wonder”. From that single casino, the group, headed by executive chairman Tan Sri Lim Kok Thay, expanded to Singapore, the UK, the US and the Bahamas.
The relentless expansion came at a price, however.
The perception that Genting was a cash cow proved to be a fallacy. Dividends started to fall, with only five sen declared for the financial year ended Dec 31, 2025 — a far cry from the 22 sen declared in 2019.
Genting fell to a historic low on Oct 9 when it called for a rights issue to raise RM1.25 billion.
It said a sum of RM800 million had been allocated to repay debts, with the balance for working capital. Of the working capital, RM280 million is for payment of interest and financing costs.
Genting’s rights issue is difficult to fathom, given its cash reserves of more than RM17.6 billion and its business, which draws thousands of tourists and high rollers.
Shareholders did not take it lightly and research analysts called for a “sell” on concerns of more rights issues to pay off its debts. As a result, the company’s share price fell to a low of RM1.38 on the next trading day.
In a reply to questions from The Edge, Genting allayed fears of further cash calls.
“No further equity fundraising is currently planned by the company,” it says.
Try telling that to analysts. CIMB Securities in a research note stated that while a rights issue does not mathematically destroy shareholders’ wealth, investors usually view such exercises negatively, as it replaces cheaper debt with more expensive equity.
“Thus, we expect a negative share price reaction, though the extent of a potential selldown may be somewhat mitigated, given that the rights [issue] is renounceable,” it said in a report.
Maybank, which has generally been positive on Genting, downgraded the stock to a “sell” after the rights issue. It expects the cash call to deliver minimal interest savings and degearing but significantly dilute earnings per share.
“We also cannot rule out more equity fundraising efforts and fewer dividends,” the research house said.
Rating agencies see the rights issue, however, as a welcome shift away from Genting’s traditional heavy reliance on debt funding to reduce and refinance its borrowings.
“It indicates shareholders’ willingness to share the deleveraging burden,” said a note from CreditSights, a research unit under Fitch Solutions.
CreditSights added, however, that Genting needs to do more than implement a rights issue.
“We see the sale of non-core assets as a vital tool to stave off a downgrade, notably the unused parcels of land in Miami.”
The land, which is held by Genting Malaysia Bhd (KL:GENM), is worth about US$1.2 billion (RM4.89 billion). The proceeds from the sale could shave off a sizeable portion of debt at group level.
On paper, Genting’s cash and debts are huge. The holding company had cash of more than RM17 billion and debts of RM45.3 billion as at end-June 2026.
Genting says, however, that just over 10% of the debts are attributed to the company while the rest are at the subsidiary level. The same is true for the cash, where the amount at the holding company is RM1.3 billion (see “No further fundraising planned for now, says Genting”).
As such, this effectively means that Genting’s debts are below RM5 billion. It is raising the RM1.25 billion to help pare off debts that are coming due next year.
In 2027, Genting has one US dollar paper amounting to US$617.5 million and three ringgit-denominated debt papers totalling some RM2.35 billion coming due.
The US dollar paper amounting to US$617.5 million is due in January. The original sum raised was US$1.5 billion via Genting Overseas Holdings Ltd (GOHL) in 2017. Part of the proceeds went towards building Resorts World Las Vegas (RWLV), a mammoth project that started in 2013 and was completed in 2021.
“GOHL redeemed US$882 million of the bonds in a tender offer in May 2026. It was funded via its concurrent US$1.25 billion debt issuance. This leaves close to US$618 million outstanding,” says Jonathan Tan, an analyst at CreditSights.
Genting has a RM300 million debt due this December. It is part of a RM3 billion medium-term note (MTN) programme to help fund the takeover of GenM late last year.
Its ringgit-denominated debt amounting to RM2.35 billion are due in March, June and December next year: The biggest tranche of RM1.5 billion is due in June while the debt coming due in March and December are RM400 million and RM450 million respectively.
The RM1.5 billion debt was issued in 2012, before the start of the construction of RWLV, and the proceeds were on-lent to the group’s subsidiaries for working capital, development expenditure and other expenses.
The ringgit debt paper of RM400 million due in March was issued in 2022 with a coupon rate of 5.19%.
The RM450 million bond due in December next year is part of a RM3 billion MTN programme that Genting raised to fund the voluntary takeover of GenM last year. Genting increased its stake in GenM to 73.9%, which cost it close to RM2.8 billion.
Analysts are unsure as to which debt issuance Genting will retire with the proceeds of the rights issue.
“We do not foresee Genting or GenM having any problems refinancing its debt papers. Together with the proceeds from the rights issue, Genting has flexibility and many options,” says a fixed income analyst.
CreditSights’ Tan expects the refinancing to come at a higher rate. “Genting’s upcoming ringgit-denominated bonds include RM750 million at Klibor (Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rate) + 1.8%. These were taken earlier mainly to finance its 23% stake acquisition in Genting Malaysia. Given the broader macro uncertainties and Genting’s worsening credit outlook, we would expect refinancing to come in at slightly higher costs [than] Klibor + 1.8%,” he says.
The RM750 million comprises RM300 million due this December and RM450 million due in December next year.
Genting says the majority of its borrowings maturing in 2027 were incurred more than 10 years ago.
“The rights issue forms part of Genting’s proactive capital management strategy to deleverage and strengthen its credit profile. Proceeds from the rights issue, together with internal cash resources, will be used to repay a portion of these borrowings, reducing reliance on debt-funded refinancing,” the company says in its email reply to The Edge.
Genting was a net cash company in 2010. At that time, its overseas operations were mainly concentrated in Singapore, with GenM expanding to the UK.
Lim was instrumental in leading Genting to win one of the two casino licences that the Singapore government awarded in December 2006. Resorts World Sentosa (RWS), which opened in 2010, proved to be a profitable diversification and is a key contributor to the group’s earnings until today.
Singapore authorities, however, keep a close watch on RWS and its management.
Although Genting Singapore is cash-rich and has no debt, Genting is unable to tap the cash, other than enjoy the consistent dividends. That is because Genting Singapore is mandated to use the cash for its RWS 2.0 expansion project, which costs about S$6.8 billion (RM19.1 billion), to be expensed until 2030.
While Genting Singapore is profitable and a key contributor to the parent company, the same cannot be said of RWLV.
Genting started its high-profile project in Las Vegas in 2013. By 2019, it was already in a net debt position and, when the RWLV was completed two years later, its gross debts were close to RM40 billion.
RWLV’s numbers remain unattractive, considering Genting’s US$4.5 billion investment in it.
Based on notes in Genting’s annual report, RWLV has been raising debt on its own, reducing its dependency on the parent company. Still, it is not clear whether RWLV will be able to refinance its debts at palatable rates without guarantees from its parent company.
That is why analysts believe that measures taken by Genting — implementing the rights issue, reducing dividend payouts — and its hopes for an improvement in earnings from Singapore and New York may not be enough to turn the red tide.

title: Cover Story: No further fundraising planned for now, says Genting
body:
This article first appeared in The Edge Malaysia Weekly on October 19, 2026 - October 25, 2026
GENTING Bhd (KL:GENTING) made a cash call on Oct 9 to raise RM1.25 billion — 53 years after its first one.
The conglomerate, which was listed in 1971, called for a rights issue in 1973.
At that time, Genting’s call for more cash from shareholders was acceptable. It was a period in which the group was still building the infrastructure to turn the casino into a holiday resort to cater for both tourists and high rollers.
The Genting Highlands Hotel (now known as Genting Skyworld Hotel), the first hotel in the highlands, was among the infrastructure being built. Since then, the group had never asked for more money from shareholders, until recently.
The current proposed rights issue, which requires minority shareholders’ approval, has not gone down well with investors, although those shares will be issued at a discount of up to 30% to the market price.
Based on last Friday’s closing of RM1.45, Genting’s market capitalisation stood at RM5.58 billion. The conglomerate’s hopes of becoming a constituent of the FBM KLCI 50 may have been dashed, as it was ranked 70th by market capitalisation.
Shareholders seldom welcome cash calls because of their dilutive effect. In Genting’s case, the rights issue has renewed investor concerns over the conglomerate’s hefty RM45.3 billion debt burden and the prospect of further fundraising exercises.
“No further equity fundraising is currently planned by the company,” says Genting.
Its debt swelled after it invested US$4.5 billion to build Resorts World Las Vegas (RWLV), a venture that has yet to deliver the returns hoped for.
Proceeds from the rights issue will go towards reducing debt incurred more than a decade ago, around the time construction of RWLV began.
In reply to questions from The Edge, Genting says although the company sits on huge cash and debts, the bulk of it is at the subsidiary level. It explains why a fundraising was needed to reduce borrowings taken more than 10 years ago.
The Edge: Why does Genting need a rights issue when it already holds more than RM17 billion in cash?
Genting: As with its debt, most of the group’s cash is held at its subsidiaries to meet their respective operating, corporate and capital expenditure requirements. The rights issue is intended to strengthen Genting’s balance sheet and financial flexibility.
Why is Genting raising just RM1.25 billion through a rights issue, with RM800 million earmarked for debt repayment, when its borrowings stand at roughly RM45 billion?
Most of the group’s debt sits at its operating subsidiaries rather than at the corporate level.
Please refer to our earlier response to Question 1. The size of the rights issue was determined after taking into consideration Genting’s internal cash resources, upcoming debt maturities, leverage and credit profile, while balancing the interests of shareholders, including the potential dilutive impact of a larger equity fundraising.
Genting had stated before that most of its debt was at the operating level. Can the company please clarify how much debt is at the respective operating levels and what is the amount accrued to Genting, the company itself?
The group’s total borrowings stood at RM45.3 billion as at June 30, 2026, of which just over 10% was attributable to Genting (the company). The balance was incurred by the subsidiaries for their respective operational, funding and capital expenditure requirements.
Is the fundraising due to borrowings taken by Genting when it undertook a mandatory general offer on Genting Malaysia?
Most of Genting’s borrowings maturing in 2027 were incurred more than 10 years ago. The rights issue forms part of Genting’s proactive capital management strategy to deleverage and strengthen its credit profile. Proceeds from the rights issue, together with internal cash resources, will be used to repay a portion of these borrowings, reducing reliance on debt-funded refinancing.
What is Genting’s cash position at the corporate level, and how much cash is held by its operating subsidiaries?
As at Dec 31, 2025, Genting had cash and cash equivalents of about RM1.3 billion at the company level. Most of the group’s cash balances were held at the operating subsidiary level and are earmarked for their respective operational, debt servicing and capital expenditure needs.
Will there be future rounds of fundraising, considering the outstanding debt of close to RM44 billion?
No further equity fundraising is currently planned by the company.
Why not sell non-core assets to reduce debt instead of pursuing a rights issue that has spooked Genting’s minority shareholders?
The group continues to actively evaluate opportunities to optimise its asset portfolio and monetise non-core assets and/or businesses, as and when appropriate, to unlock value, improve capital efficiency and support its long-term strategic objectives. While asset monetisation initiatives are already underway, such transactions typically require time to execute and realise value. The rights issue enables the group to strengthen its balance sheet and address near-term funding objectives in a timely and prudent manner, while pursuing asset monetisation opportunities in parallel.
In the announcement of its proposed rights issue, Genting specified a discount to its share price. But its share price has fallen significantly since the announcement. Will this affect the proposed discount for the rights issue?
As stated in the company announcements, the board intends to fix the issue price at a discount ranging between 25% and 30% to the theoretical ex-rights price. The discount range was arrived at after taking into account numerous factors set out in the announcements and is in line with discount levels adopted in other rights issue transactions. The recent share price movement is not expected to affect the intended discount range.

title: Genting Share Price Dives 24% In Last 10 Days As Rights Issue Raises Cash Flow Concerns
body:
Genting Bhd’s share price has plunged nearly 24.5% in just 10 days, as investors continue to sell down the gaming and hospitality conglomerate following its announcement of a RM1.25 billion rights issue to repay borrowings and strengthen working capital.

The stock declined from RM1.88 on Oct 9 to RM1.42 on Monday (Oct 19), reflecting sustained selling pressure and growing concerns over the group’s debt burden, financing requirements and potential earnings dilution.

The sell-off intensified on Oct 12, when Genting shares plunged 22.9% to RM1.45, wiping out more than RM1.6 billion in market capitalisation in a single trading session.

The sharp decline reflects investor unease over the proposed fundraising exercise, which has raised questions about the group’s financial flexibility despite its extensive international gaming and hospitality operations.

Under the proposed renounceable rights issue announced on Oct 9, Genting intends to raise approximately RM1.25 billion, with RM800 million allocated to repay existing borrowings.

Another RM429.5 million will be used for working capital, while RM20.5 million is earmarked for expenses related to the exercise.

In a subsequent clarification to Bursa Malaysia, Genting disclosed that RM280 million of the working capital allocation would be used to meet interest payments and other financing-related expenses. The remaining RM149.5 million would fund operational and administrative requirements.

The group had total borrowings of approximately RM45.25 billion as at June 30, 2026, alongside cash and cash equivalents of RM17.64 billion.

Genting expects the proposed debt repayment to generate annual interest savings of approximately RM41.3 million

Although the exercise would strengthen its capital structure, the decision to raise fresh equity has heightened investor concerns about the group’s financing requirements.

Genting has indicated that the rights shares would be priced at a discount of between 25% and 30% to the theoretical ex-rights price, with an illustrative issue price of RM1.30 per share.

CIMB Securities previously cautioned that the proposed exercise could dilute Genting’s core earnings per share by approximately 17% to 18% for financial years 2027 and 2028.

The potential dilution presents a challenge for existing shareholders, particularly those who may need to commit additional capital to maintain their proportional ownership.

The fundraising exercise is expected to be completed in the first quarter of 2027, subject to the necessary approvals.

title: Genting’s debt, equity divide
author: BHUPINDER SINGH
body:
Genting Bhd has proposed a rights issue to raise fresh cash amid rising credit costs pressures.
The corporate exercise is the first of its kind in its 55-year listing history. The fundraising comes at a time when the group’s leverage metrics are stretched by its expansionary ambitions.
Genting is expected to spend more than RM9bil in capital expenditure (capex) annually over the next three years to expand key gaming properties, especially in Singapore and New York.
Such plans have seen its debt load rise to RM45.3bil as of endJune, with a real impact on its finances.
High finance costs and capital structure obligations consume a sizeable share of operating profits, limiting net margin expansion. That, in turn, is eating into its dividend payout rates and driving away equity investors.
Rating agencies like Fitch Ratings had already downgraded the company to BBB- last month, just one notch above junk bond, or high-yield, grade.
The agency warned that it expects the pace of Genting’s deleveraging to be slow due to substantial capex spending, while the ramp-up at Genting New York LLC (GenNY) was underperforming, compounded by a gradual recovery across the group’s other gaming operations. Gaming accounts for 85% of total group revenue.
S&P Global Ratings flagged that Genting has no more buffer for earnings disappointments, warning that its funds from operations to net debt ratio of around 16% remains significantly below the agency’s 20% downgrade threshold.
Genting’s management appears ready to defend its investment-grade status, with the rights issue one option it is pursuing. The reason is economic: the company needs access to debt markets, and a further downgrade would be expensive.
A fallen angel will have to pay an extra 50 basis points to 100 basis points in funding costs as its pool of investors narrows.
As it stands Genting must address roughly RM6.27bil in major bond redemptions over the next 18-month window.
With the threat of a crossover rating still present, the rights issue is viewed as a morale-boosting signal from its main shareholders that they are ready to back the company’s deleveraging efforts with cash.
Analysts are also not overly concerned about Genting’s level of financial stress.
“We see the RM1.25bil rights issue more as a balance-sheet management exercise rather than a funding option of last resort. Genting may also consider asset disposals and other funding avenues to preserve financial flexibility,” an equity analyst with a local brokerage tells StarBiz 7.
He adds that the rights issue only modestly improves leverage, and that the bigger concern is that fresh recapitalisation may be needed before Genting’s cash flow strengthens meaningfully.
He, however, admits that it is difficult to say whether Genting can continue accessing the ringgit bond market on attractive terms, but taking on more debt may not address the bigger issue of high leverage and rating pressure.
A fixed-income fund manager told StarBiz 7 that access to the ringgit or US dollar bond markets remains to Genting, but at a price that reflects investor expectations rather than its existing credit rating.
It got a taste of that in April, when Genting raised US$1.5bil through the issuance of two tranches of unsecured subordinated perpetual bonds (sub perps) amid the threat of a downgrade in its credit ratings.
The PerpNC5.5 (perpetual non-call 5.5-year bond) and PerpNC10 tranches offered coupon rates of 7.65% and 8.3%, respectively. The high yields saw the perps oversubscribed by more than 2.2 times.
While equity investors sold Genting shares following the rights issue announcement, and analysts either cut their target price and/or calls on Genting, bond analysts appear calm about the latest announcement.
CreditSights, a Fitch Solution company, maintained its “outperform” recommendation on Genting’s sub perps and “market perform” recommendation on its more senior debt.
The credit research firm said the most effective and likely tool for Genting to avert junk status is to monetise its non-core real estate assets.
It identified the group’s prime undeveloped land holdings in Miami, Florida – estimated to be worth over US$1bil – as the primary liquidity lever capable of generating immediate cash to pay down debt and restore leverage ratios.
This divide between bond and equity investors is due to capital structure. Debt holders tend to have more legal right to claims, while equity owners are last in line.
Furthermore, Genting’s assets of over RM100bil are one reason debt investors appear to welcome the exercise, while equity investors and analysts have viewed the rights issues from a dilution perspective.
Hence, the analyst is keeping his eye on the group’s cash flow trends.
“We do not rule out another equity raising if operating cash flow disappoints and capex remains elevated. That said, Genting may still have other options, including asset disposals, dividend restraint and alternative funding avenues.
“Ultimately, the need for further equity will depend on how quickly its major investments translate into stronger earnings and cash flow,” he says.
The 24%, or 45 sen, drop in Genting’s share price following the rights issue announcement, to RM1.43 sen at last look, has attracted buying by the founders and controlling shareholder, the Lim family.
The family, which holds a 45.1% stake, has irrevocably committed to subscribing to its full entitlement, amounting to RM564mil.
With the stock trading at a 25-year low, the family has also been buying shares on the open market, Genting’s exchange filing show.
The group aims to allocate RM800mil of the rights issue proceeds to repay unspecified debt and RM430mil for general working capital, with the flexibility to redirect RM280mil of the latter towards interest payments, bringing the amount available for debt repayment to as much as RM1.1bil.
Genting’s consolidated borrowings of RM45.25bil comprise RM9.68bil in short-term obligations and RM35.58bil in long-term debt, with interest rates ranging from 3.88% to 8.45% per annum.
CreditSights, meanwhile, believes a further equity injection will be unnecessary in the short term.
“We think Genting and Genting Malaysia Bhd can refinance upcoming ringgit bonds via new ringgit bond issues, and do not think it is justified to raise a much higher cost of funding via equity to repay ringgit bonds carrying 5% coupons,” it stated in its report.

title: Genting loses its lustre
body:
KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 17): A generation of investors grew up believing that Genting Bhd (KL:GENTING) was a cash-generating machine where nothing can go wrong even during the worst of times.
It survived economic turmoil and the pandemic. A stock favoured by 'mom and pops' for its regular dividends, the cash from Genting’s only casino in Malaysia was enough to fund its expansion overseas and keep shareholders happy.
From a single casino in Genting Highlands, Pahang, the group, headed by executive chairman Tan Sri Lim Kok Thay, expanded to Singapore, the UK, the US and Bahamas.
The relentless expansion comes with a price.
Genting fell to the lowest point in its history last week when it called for a rights issue to raise RM1.25 billion.
With a cash hoard of more than RM17.6 billion and a business that draws thousands of tourists and high rollers, Genting’s cash call is unfathomable.
Shareholders did not take it lightly, with research analysts calling for a sell on concerns of more cash calls in the future to pay off debts. Consequently, Genting’s share price fell to a 52-week low of RM1.38 last Wednesday before recovering some lost ground.
The company says that there are no further cash calls being planned currently.
But investors and analysts have turned negative on Genting.
However, there is also a view that the rights issue is a welcome shift away from Genting’s traditional heavy reliance on debt funding to reduce and refinance its borrowings. It effectively indicates that shareholders are prepared to fork out money to share the deleveraging burden.
However, rating agencies say that Genting needs to do more than a rights issue. A sale of non-core assets is crucial to deleverage.

title: Genting chairman buys more shares as stock nears two-decade low
body:
KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 16): Genting Bhd (KL:GENTING) executive chairman Tan Sri Lim Kok Thay’s private investment vehicle, Kien Huat Realty Sdn Bhd, has acquired additional shares in the group as its stock hovers near its two-decade lows.
The latest acquisitions bring Lim's deemed interest in Genting to 45.24% or 1.74 billion shares, according to the group’s bourse filings.
The latest acquisitions of a total of 422,500 shares happened on Oct 14 and 15 at RM1.4940, RM1.3919 apiece respectively, for a total transaction value of RM596,924.50.
Lim has raised his deemed interest in Genting by about 6.42 million shares amid the stock's sell-off in the wake of its proposed RM1.25 billion rights issue announcement last week.
The stock has fallen 22.9% since the announcement, ending flat at RM1.45 on Friday for a market capitalisation RM5.6 billion.
Meanwhile, group CEO Datuk Seri Tan Kong Han acquired an additional 150,000 shares in the group.
Tan acquired 50,000 shares at RM1.45 apiece on Oct 13 and another 100,000 at RM1.42 apiece for a total of RM214,500.
This amount is on top of the 400,000 shares he acquired on Oct 12 amounting to RM624,000.
Following the latest acquisition by Tan who is also the president and an executive director of the group, he now holds 2.04 million shares which represent a 0.053% direct stake in the group. He still holds an indirect stake of 0.003% or equivalent to indirect stake.
Of the RM1.25 billion proposed fundraising, Genting has earmarked RM800 million to repay borrowings, RM280 million to pay interest and other financing costs, RM149.5 million for general operation requirements and RM20.5 million to cover expenses related to the exercise.
The rights issue will be at a discount of 25% to 30% to Genting's theoretical ex-rights price, based on the company's proposal.

title: Genting ‘itching to invest’ further in UK market but wary of looming MGD hike
author: Kathryn Evans
body:
Genting ‘itching to invest’ further in UK market but wary of looming MGD hike
On Wednesday, leading figures from the UK’s casino sector issued a warning that the possible doubling of machine games duty (MGD), combined with wider economic pressures, threatens to impede investment and put jobs at risk, just as the industry seeks to modernise.
The comments were made during a panel discussion held at the Hippodrome Casino in London featuring executives from major operators Rank Group, Genting Casinos and the Hippodrome, alongside representatives from the Night Time Industries Association (NTIA) and consultancy Regulus Partners.
Investment is key
Richard Harris, CEO of Rank Group, expressed concern over the cumulative impact of increased taxation, tighter regulation and rising operating costs.
“In my four and a half years, we’ve closed four of our venues,” Harris said. He attributed closures to the challenging financial environment caused by a high cost base, escalating taxes and regulatory tightening, stressing these factors had collectively strained profitability and cash generation.
Harris highlighted that speculation around higher taxes had already impacted investment decisions. This view was echoed by Paul Willcock, COO of Genting Casinos, who described the prospect of MGD hikes as “keeping us all awake”.
The potential MGD hike from 20% to 40% was proposed by thinktank the Social Market Foundation a few months ago and has been reported as being possibly on the agenda for the government’s upcoming autumn budget.
However, the sector has fiercely opposed the proposal warning it could be detrimental to their retail businesses.
In September, Betfred owner Fred Done emphasised that such a tax rise would lead his company to close 495 of its shops within a year, resulting in the loss of 2,575 jobs and roughly £67 million in foregone tax revenue for the Exchequer.
“If we can get some relaxation or at least certainty on that, then investment will flow,” Willcock told the audience.
He emphasised Genting’s ongoing global investment efforts, noting the operator was ready and willing to expand in the UK, as long as a stable fiscal and regulatory climate is in place.
“Genting has invested $5 billion on the Las Vegas Strip in the last five years. Spent $5 billion in New York and $3 billion in Singapore,” he said.
“It is itching to invest in the United Kingdom.”
Simon Thomas, executive chairman of the Hippodrome, framed the issue in terms of industry confidence. He said operators needed assurance that “playing conditions” and the regulatory and financial environment would remain stable over typical investment horizons of three to seven years.
Harris concurred, summarising that “profit is the source of future investment” It is consistent conditions that enable operators to generate and deploy profits effectively.
Modernisation reforms yield positive signs but require time
The panel welcomed the Gambling Commission’s 2025 land-based modernisation reforms, which increased the number of slot machines per casino from 20 to up to 80 and relaxed ancillary betting rules.
Rank Group’s Harris revealed that the company had expanded its machine estate by approximately 65% from 1,400 to 2,250 machines, investing £15 million in a single venue, driven by these reforms.
However, panellists cautioned that these changes require time to fully embed and stressed that tax stability must accompany regulatory liberalisation for the sector to flourish.
Dan Waugh, partner at Regulus Partners, highlighted the importance of measuring whether reforms had improved customer experience and broadened appeal: “Are these better places to go to as a result of the regulated reforms? And also, is the experience more widely attractive?”
A huge drop in staffing should MGD rise proceed
The casino sector has identified a planned investment pipeline of roughly £200 million over the next few years, the panel said.
Michael Kill, CEO of the NTIA, emphasised the potential wider economic benefits of sustained casino investment, including supporting high streets, night-time economies, jobs and local supply chains.
In a report presented by the NTIA at the panel, Kill revealed that out of responders (formed of a mixture of casino attendees and the general public) 58% identified the casino as their primary reason for visiting an area, with 55% stating they would likely not have visited the area without the casino’s presence.
Additionally, the NTIA found that if MGD did rise, job losses both direct and indirect could reach around 3,800 nationally. A survey involving 23 operators indicated that with a tax rise, 95.7% would reduce staffing levels and 91.3% would cut investment in venues.
Notably, 60.9% might be forced to close a venue outright.
Putting people at the forefront
Representatives underscored casinos’ role as significant employers and valued community contributors.
Willcock noted that Genting employs about 3,500 people in the UK and outlined rigorous training processes. “There’s significant training, six weeks training before anybody can go anywhere near a casino table,” he said.
Both Kill and Waugh elaborated on casinos’ broader societal impact, highlighting enhanced perceptions of safety in town centres during late-night hours and the use of venues for community meetings.
Kill pointed out an often-overlooked benefit: “People coming after midnight actually felt safe because of the service levels, because of the engagement, the lighting, etc.”
Industry calls on government for stability and time
The panellists collectively urged the government to allow its 2025 reforms to fully take effect without approving immediate additional tax increases.
Kill pleaded for “a chance to bed in” these reforms and recognition of casinos as integral to extended hospitality offers capable of supporting 24-hour economies.
Willcock and Harris emphasised that a clear, durable fiscal framework would act as a catalyst for further large-scale investments.
Waugh cautioned against policy driven excessively by “public health dogma”. He advocated instead for balanced regulation that protects consumers while enabling sustainable business growth.
Regulus released an analysis recently that estimated the horse racing industry could face a loss of around a third of its annual revenue – £92 million – should the duty rise.

title: Genting to allocate RM280mil from rights issue for interest, financing costs
author: The Star
body:
KUALA LUMPUR: Genting Bhd has earmarked RM280 million from its proposed RM1.25 billion renounceable rights issue to pay interest and other financing-related costs on the group’s borrowings and funding arrangements.
The group said in a stock filing exchange that the allocation forms part of the RM429.5 million set aside for working capital requirements.
The remaining RM149.5 million will be used to meet general working capital requirements of the company and its unlisted subsidiaries, including employee-related costs, professional fees, regulatory and compliance charges, tax liabilities, as well as operating and administrative expenses.
Genting said the allocation was based on the group’s anticipated funding and operational requirements, adding that the amounts allocated to the various working capital components may be adjusted according to its operational, business and funding needs.
The filing was made in response to queries from Bursa Malaysia dated Oct 13, 2026, seeking clarification on the proposed rights issue.
On the proposed discount of between 25 per cent and 30 per cent to the theoretical ex-rights price (TERP), based on the five-day volume-weighted average price of Genting shares preceding the price-fixing date, the group said the range was determined following discussions with its principal adviser.
The considerations included the size of the proposed rights issue, prevailing market conditions, the historical trading performance and liquidity of Genting shares, discount levels adopted in previous rights issues, and underwriting appetite for the remaining open portion of the rights shares.
Genting said the discount was intended to make the rights shares more attractive, encourage shareholder participation, reward entitled shareholders for their continued support, facilitate a higher subscription level and improve the certainty of raising the targeted gross proceeds.
On Oct 9, Genting announced plans to raise RM1.25 billion through the proposed renounceable rights issue, with RM800 million earmarked for debt repayment and RM20.5 million for expenses related to the exercise. - Bernama

title: Stock Today: Genting Rises 1.41% Following Rights Issue Clarification
body:
Genting Bhd shares rose 1.41% to RM1.44 as of 3.46pm, gaining two sen from the previous close of RM1.42, as investors continued to monitor the group’s proposed RM1.25 billion rights issue.

The stock opened at RM1.43 and traded between RM1.40 and RM1.45 during the session, with 15.86 million shares changing hands.

Genting’s latest share price movement follows its clarification on Wednesday regarding the proposed rights issue, including its rationale for offering a discount of 25% to 30% to the theoretical ex-rights price to encourage shareholder participation and improve fundraising certainty.

The group plans to raise RM1.25 billion through the renounceable rights issue, with approximately RM800 million earmarked for debt repayment and RM429.5 million allocated for working capital requirements.

Of the working capital allocation, RM280 million is intended to cover interest payments and other financing-related expenses, while the remaining RM149.5 million will support general operating and administrative needs.

Genting said the proposed discount was determined after considering the fundraising exercise’s size, its historical share price performance, trading liquidity and investor appetite.

title: Genting Defends 25%-30% Rights Issue Discount, Earmarks RM280 Million For Financing Costs
body:
Genting Bhd has clarified that the proposed 25% to 30% discount for its RM1.25 billion rights issue is intended to encourage shareholder participation and improve the certainty of raising the targeted proceeds amid prevailing market conditions.

The group said the discount was determined following discussions with its principal adviser, taking into consideration the size of the fundraising exercise, Genting’s historical share price performance, trading liquidity and investor appetite.

The clarification was in response to Bursa Securities’ query concerning Genting’s proposed renounceable rights issue announced on Oct 9.

Genting said the discount would be calculated against the theoretical ex-rights price (TERP), based on the five-day volume-weighted average market price of its shares preceding the price-fixing date.

The group explained that the discount was designed to provide existing shareholders with a meaningful incentive to subscribe for their entitlements or apply for additional rights shares.

It also considered discounts offered in comparable rights issue exercises and underwriting appetite for the portion of shares not covered by shareholder commitments.

According to Genting, the pricing approach is intended to encourage higher subscription levels while improving the certainty of securing the RM1.25 billion in gross proceeds.

In response to Bursa Malaysia’s request for further details on the proposed utilisation of proceeds, Genting disclosed that RM429.5 million would be allocated towards working capital requirements.

Of this amount, RM280 million will be used to meet interest payments and other financing-related expenses associated with the group’s borrowings and funding arrangements.

The remaining RM149.5 million will support general working capital requirements of Genting and its unlisted subsidiaries.

These include employee-related expenses, professional fees, regulatory and compliance charges, tax liabilities, and other operating and administrative costs incurred in the ordinary course of business.

The financing cost allocation represents approximately 65.2% of the proposed working capital provision.

Genting said the breakdown was based on anticipated operational and funding requirements, although the actual allocation could be adjusted depending on business needs.

The proposed RM1.25 billion rights issue also includes approximately RM800 million earmarked for debt repayment, as outlined in Genting’s earlier announcement.

The fundraising exercise comes as the group seeks to manage its financing obligations and strengthen financial flexibility.

Genting stressed that the proposed discount was intended to reward existing shareholders for their continued support while facilitating a successful fundraising exercise.

title: In response to Bursa query, Genting says will use RM280m from working capital portion of rights issue for interest costs
body:
KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 14): Genting Bhd (KL:GENTING) has earmarked RM280 million from its proposed RM1.25 billion rights issue to pay interest and other financing costs.
The sum will be utilised from the proposed working capital allocation of RM429.5 million, Genting said in its reply to Bursa Malaysia’s queries on the proposed rights issue on Wednesday.
The remaining RM149.5 million would be allocated for general working capital requirements, it said, to cover expenses such as employee-related costs, professional fees, regulatory and compliance charges, tax liabilities and operating and administrative expenses.
The allocation among working capital components may be adjusted over time, according to its operational, business and funding requirements, it added.
Apart from the breakdown of the working capital allocation, Bursa Malaysia had requested additional information on the basis for the proposed 25% to 30% discount to the theoretical ex-rights price (TERP), based on the five-day volume-weighted average price of Genting shares preceding the price-fixing date.
Genting said the discount range was determined after discussions with its principal adviser, taking into account the size of the rights issue, prevailing market conditions, historical share price performance and liquidity, discount levels adopted in previous rights issues and underwriting appetite for remaining open portion of the rights shares.
This also takes into account of the need to provide entitled shareholders with meaningful incentive to subscribe for their right shares and or apply for excess right shares, it added.
The discount is intended to encourage shareholders to subscribe rights shares, reward entitled shareholders for their support, facilitate a higher subscription level and improve certainty of raising the targeted gross proceeds of RM1.25 billion.
The clarification follows Genting’s announcement last Friday (Oct 9) that it plans to raise RM1.25 billion through a renounceable rights issue. It has earmarked the other RM800 million to repay borrowings and RM20.5 million to cover expenses related to the right issue exercise.
Genting said the RM800 million debt repayment could generate potential interest savings of about RM41.3 million annually, based on the group’s weighted average interest rate of 5.16% for short-term borrowings as at June 30, 2026.
The group had total borrowings of RM45.25 billion as at June 30, 2026, comprising RM9.68 billion in short-term borrowings and RM35.58 billion in long-term borrowings. The interest rates on its borrowings ranged from 3.88% to 8.45% per annum.
Genting had cash and cash equivalents of RM17.64 billion as at end-June 30, 2026.
The proposed RM1.25 billion fundraising is based on an illustrative issue price of RM1.30 per rights share.
Genting shares fell two sen or 1.39% to close at RM1.42 on Wednesday — its lowest since April 2003 — as over 29 million shares exchanged hands.
The company has lost about RM1.77 billion or nearly 25% of its market value since announcing its proposed rights issue. At RM1.42, the group is valued at RM5.47 billion.
The stock has more than halved so far this year from RM2.92 at the start of 2026.
In a separate filing, Genting executive chairman Tan Sri Lim Kok Thay acquired six million shares in the group on Oct 12 at RM1.494 per share through his private investment vehicle Kien Huat Realty Sdn Bhd, bringing his deemed interest in Genting to 45.228% or 1.74 billion shares.

title: CreditSights: Genting Bhd rights issue a positive but small step towards deleveraging
body:
Financial research firm CreditSights says it views Genting Bhd’s newly announced rights issue positively from a credit standpoint but noted the improvement to credit metrics is modest.
In a Tuesday note, CreditSights observed that the right issue, which aims to raise MYR1.25 billion (US$306 million), marks a “welcome shift away” from the group’s traditional reliance on debt funding and “signals shareholders’ willingness to share the deleveraging burden.”
This comes with the group holding MYR26.1 billion (US$6.4 billion) in net borrowings as of 31 March 2026 and major capex commitments that include its US$5.5 billion expansion of Resorts World New York City via Genting Malaysia and US$5 billion reimagining of Resorts World Sentosa via Genting Singapore.
The rights issue could, the research firm explain, reduce leverage by between 0.2x and 0.3x to around 4.3x.
While shares in Genting Bhd fell by around 20% following the rights announcement, CreditSights said it does not expect any shareholder resistance given it only requires an ordinary resolution and has strong backing by the Lim family, whose 45.1% stake provides a substantial voting bloc in favor of the rights issue. The Lim family has also committed to subscribe for MYR564 billion (US$138 million), representing their full stake, with likely to be used to address upcoming bond maturities.
CreditSights pointed out that the Lim family’s subscription ensures the public float remains above 25% and that a mandatory takeover offer of Genting Bhd will not be pursued, with a mandatory offer triggered if the Lim family acquires over 2% of additional voting stake within any rolling 6-month period.
It also believes the group’s current debt situation will prevent any further moves by Genting Bhd to pursue any debt-funded takeover attempts of Genting Malaysia in the next 12 to 18 months in order to preserve balance sheet strength and avoid further leverage and rating downgrade risks.
Genting Bhd last year lifted its stake in the Malaysian subsidiary – which counts the New York assets as well as Malaysia’s Resorts World Genting among its core assets – from 49.36% to 73.13% via a voluntary takeover offer. This fell short of the 75% required to take Genting Malaysia private, although the parent has since lifted its stake to 73.8% via on-market purchases.
Instead, CreditSights expects the group to focus further on deleveraging opportunities, among them non-core asset sales such as its unused Miami land parcels.
While dividend curtailments, perpetual security issuances and earnings improvements are viewed as insufficient to turn the tide amid the very heavy capex pipeline, CreditSights remains positive on the long-term outlook – despite S&P Global Ratings recently warning that Genting Bhd is at risk of becoming a “fallen angel.”
Mitigants to this include positive earnings takeaways such as robust ramp in New York and improvement in Las Vegas and Singapore, dividend prudence, robust liquidity and the possible Miami land sale.

title: Genting CEO buys shares as stock nears two-decade low
body:
KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 13): Genting Bhd (KL:GENTING) CEO Datuk Seri Tan Kong Han bought 400,000 shares in the group on Monday, when its stock fell to a near two-decade low.
According to a filing with Bursa Malaysia on Tuesday, Tan acquired 200,000 shares at RM1.58 apiece and another 200,000 shares at RM1.54 apiece on Oct 12, for a total of RM624,000.
His previous share purchase was on Sept 29, when he acquired 200,000 shares at RM1.87 apiece.
Following the latest acquisitions, Tan, who is also president and an executive director at the group, holds 1.89 million shares directly, representing a 0.049% stake in the group. He also has an indirect or deemed interest in 100,000 shares, equivalent to 0.003%.
Tan’s purchases came as Genting lost more than RM2 billion in market value on Monday, with its share price falling to RM1.45.
The selling pressure followed Genting’s Oct 9 announcement of a RM1.25 billion rights issue to reduce debt. While some analysts warned of earnings and dividend dilution, others said it would provide a cheaper way to raise funds amid rising borrowing costs and major commitments in the US and Singapore.
On Tuesday, CreditSights said the group may need to sell non-core assets, particularly unused land to reduce its debt burden and avoid further credit rating downgrades.
Genting’s shares remained under pressure on Tuesday, hitting an intraday high of RM1.50 before falling to an intraday low of RM1.44 and closing at that level, down one sen or 0.69%.
The stock was among the most actively traded on Bursa Malaysia, with about 20.7 million shares changing hands.

title: Genting Bhd asset sales key despite US$306mln rights issue: CreditSights
body:
Malaysia’s Genting Bhd will in likelihood need to “sell non-core assets” to stave off further credit-rating downgrades, despite a proposed MYR1.25-billion (US$305.8-million) rights issue, says CreditSights. The institution views the rights issuance as positive but thinks it will have only “modest impact” on the group’s credit metrics.

The credit research provider highlighted possible disposal of unused land parcels in Miami, in the United States, as a potential source of funds to reduce debt. It also expects Genting Bhd to avoid further debt-funded attempts to acquire shares in subsidiary Genting Malaysia Bhd over the next 12 to 18 months.

“We believe non-core asset sales will be the main tool to stave off downgrade risks, notably the unused Miami land parcels,” wrote analysts Jonathan Tan, Jun Jie, and Lakshmanan R in a Monday report.

CreditSights said dividend reductions, perpetual securities issuance and earnings improvements – particularly in New York, Singapore and Las Vegas – would be insufficient to offset the pressure from the group’s “heavy capital expenditure pipeline”.

Genting Bhd is the parent of Genting Singapore Ltd, which runs the Resorts World Sentosa casino complex in Singapore.

Genting Bhd is also the parent of Genting Malaysia Bhd, which runs that country’s only licensed casino complex, Resorts World Genting. Genting Malaysia also operates casinos in the United States, the Bahamas, the United Kingdom, and Egypt.

CreditSights said it was “cautiously hopeful” that Genting Bhd could accelerate a sale of the unused Miami land for potentially more than US$1 billion.

Genting Bhd had sought to sell four Miami land parcels for approximately US$1.23 billion in 2023, but the transaction did not proceed. S&P Global Ratings said last month that a disposal at a similar valuation could improve the group’s funds from operations-to-debt ratio by between 3 and 4 percentage points.

The global casino operator and plantations business announced its proposed rights issue on Friday, with MYR800 million earmarked for debt repayment and approximately MYR429.5 million for working capital. The exercise is expected to be completed in the first quarter of 2027.

CreditSights described the fundraising as a welcome shift from Genting’s traditionally “heavier reliance on borrowing,” signalling shareholders’ willingness to share the burden of reducing debt.

But it estimated that net leverage would decline by only 0.2 to 0.3 times, to approximately 4.3 times.

The institution said the risk of Genting Bhd losing its investment-grade rating at S&P was “slightly narrower but still pertinent,” despite management’s repeated commitment to preserve it.

Regarding Genting Malaysia, CreditSights expects the parent to refrain from further debt-funded stake acquisitions for the next 12 to 18 months to preserve its balance sheet and avoid additional leverage and rating pressure.

Genting Bhd’s previous takeover offer closed in December 2025 without achieving the 75-percent shareholding threshold needed to trigger delisting. Subsequent purchases lifted its interest to approximately 73.86 percent, as reported by GGRAsia.

CreditSights’ latest assessment suggests another debt-funded privatisation effort is unlikely in the near term. Despite the downgrade concerns, the research provider continued to see low refinancing risk for the group’s US$618-million bond maturing in January 2027. It cited available cash and access to bond and loan markets as potential funding sources.

title: Stock Today: Genting Edges Up After 22% Rout On Rights Issue
body:
Genting Bhd shares edged higher in midday trading, recovering slightly after plunging 22% in the previous session amid concerns over its proposed RM1.25 billion rights issue.

The counter gained one sen, or 0.69%, to RM1.46 as at 12.07pm, after opening at RM1.45 and moving between RM1.44 and RM1.50. Trading volume stood at 13.2 million shares.

The modest recovery followed Monday’s sharp sell-off, which saw the stock fall from RM1.88 on Friday to RM1.45 as investors assessed the potential impact of the fundraising exercise on shareholder value and earnings.

Genting plans to raise RM1.25 billion through a proposed one-for-four renounceable rights issue, with the new shares expected to be priced at a 25% to 30% discount to the theoretical ex-rights price. The exercise is targeted for completion in the first quarter of 2027, subject to shareholder approval.

Of the proceeds, RM800 million is earmarked for debt repayment, while about RM429.5 million will go towards general working capital and RM20.5 million towards expenses related to the exercise.

CIMB Securities has warned that the exercise could dilute Genting’s core earnings per share by 17% to 18% in financial years 2027 and 2028, although lower debt could generate interest savings.

CreditSights, meanwhile, said the fundraising should strengthen Genting’s balance sheet and ease refinancing pressures, but cautioned that its elevated leverage and substantial capital expenditure commitments continued to pose credit rating risks.

The proposed rights issue comes as Genting seeks to improve its financial flexibility while navigating challenges across its gaming and hospitality operations.

title: Genting may need to sell non-core assets to avert a credit-rating downgrade — CreditSights
body:
KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 13): Genting Bhd (KL:GENTING) may need to sell non-core assets, particularly unused land, to reduce its debt burden and avoid further credit-rating downgrades, according to CreditSights.
The credit research firm said Genting's proposed RM1.25 billion rights issue was a welcome move to reduce its reliance on borrowing, although it expects only a modest improvement in the group's financial position.
"We believe non-core asset sales will be the main tool to stave off downgrade risks," CreditSights said in a report.
The firm warned that Genting remains at risk of losing its investment-grade credit rating, given its heavy debt burden and substantial spending commitments.
It also identified possible dividend cuts, further fundraising and stronger earnings as ways for Genting to improve its finances.
CreditSights highlighted a US$618 million (about RM2.5 billion) bond maturing in January 2027, although it expects Genting to manage the repayment through existing cash and potentially fresh borrowings.
The firm also flagged Genting's heavy investment in its Resorts World New York City casino expansion as a risk, particularly if the spending fails to generate sufficient earnings.
While it noted an earnings recovery at Resorts World Las Vegas in the first half of 2026, sustaining that improvement remains important to the group's financial outlook.
CreditSights also expects Genting to avoid further debt-funded attempts to increase its stake in Genting Malaysia Bhd (KL:GENM) over the next 12 to 18 months to preserve its financial strength.
Genting currently owns about 73.8% of Genting Malaysia, which operates Resorts World Genting and gaming businesses overseas.
In October 2025, Genting launched a RM6.7 billion takeover offer at RM2.35 per share to acquire the remaining Genting Malaysia shares it did not own, with the aim of potentially taking the subsidiary private.
The offer closed in December without achieving privatisation, although Genting increased its shareholding to 73.13%.
The latest assessment follows Genting's announcement last Friday of a RM1.25 billion rights issue, mainly to repay borrowings and strengthen working capital.
CreditSights expects the exercise to secure shareholder approval, supported by the Lim family's commitment to subscribe for its full entitlement. The family collectively holds a 45.1% stake in Genting.
The announcement sent Genting shares plunging nearly 23% to RM1.45 on Monday, their lowest since April 2007.
Shares of Genting were up three sen or 2.07% at RM1.48 as at 10.32am on Tuesday, valuing the group at RM5.74 billion.
CreditSights maintained its "outperform" recommendation on Genting's US dollar perpetual securities and "market perform" recommendation on its senior debt.

title: Genting’s RM1.25 Billion Rights Issue Positive For Credit Profile But Downgrade Risks Remain, CreditSights
body:
Genting Bhd’s proposed RM1.25 billion rights issue is expected to strengthen the group’s balance sheet and ease refinancing pressures, although its elevated debt burden and substantial capital expenditure commitments will continue to pose credit rating risks, according to CreditSights, a Fitch Solutions company.

In its Oct 12 report, CreditSights said the fundraising exercise represented a welcome shift away from Genting’s traditional reliance on debt financing, particularly as the group faces significant debt maturities in 2027.

The research house expects the rights issue to reduce Genting’s pro forma net leverage by approximately 0.2 to 0.3 times to 4.3 times.

However, it cautioned that the improvement would remain modest relative to the group’s overall debt obligations.

CreditSights maintained its Outperform recommendation on Genting’s US dollar subordinated perpetual securities and Market Perform recommendations on its senior bonds and Genting Malaysia’s bonds.

Genting plans to raise RM1.25 billion through a proposed one-for-four rights issue, with the issue price expected to be set at a 25% to 30% discount to the theoretical ex-rights price.

The exercise, subject to shareholder approval, is expected to be completed in the first quarter of 2027.

Of the proceeds, approximately RM800 million will be allocated towards debt repayment, while RM430 million will be used for general working capital, interest or tax payments.

CreditSights noted that Genting would have flexibility to reallocate approximately RM313 million between debt repayment and working capital requirements, potentially increasing debt repayment to RM1.11 billion.

The research house expects Genting to use the proceeds to repay either its ringgit-denominated bonds or a US$618 million bond issued through GOHL Capital Ltd maturing in January 2027.

It nevertheless expects the US dollar bond to carry relatively low refinancing risk, citing the group’s access to cash resources and international bond and loan markets.

CreditSights said Genting’s major shareholder and promoter, the founding Lim family, had committed to subscribing for its full entitlement under the rights issue.

The commitment amounts to approximately RM564 million, representing 45.1% of the proposed fundraising exercise.

The research house expects the rights issue to secure shareholder approval, noting that the proposal requires an ordinary resolution supported by more than 50% of votes cast.

The Lim family’s substantial shareholding commitment is expected to provide significant support for the exercise.

CreditSights also noted that the proposed rights issue would maintain the group’s public shareholding spread above the minimum 25% requirement.

Despite viewing the rights issue positively, CreditSights warned that Genting continues to face heightened credit rating risks due to its leveraged financial position and substantial investment commitments.

The research house expects the fundraising exercise to improve Genting’s funds-from-operations-to-net-debt ratio by approximately 0.2 to 0.3 percentage points.

However, the projected ratio would remain below the 20% threshold identified by S&P Global Ratings as a potential downgrade trigger.

CreditSights said further measures could be necessary to protect Genting’s investment-grade credit rating, including non-core asset disposals, dividend reductions and additional financing initiatives.

It highlighted Genting’s unused Miami land parcels as potential disposal assets that could generate more than US$1 billion to support debt reduction.

The research house also expects Genting to avoid further debt-funded attempts to increase its stake in Genting Malaysia over the next 12 to 18 months, allowing the group to preserve its balance sheet and contain leverage.

CreditSights noted that Genting’s recent operating performance had shown some encouraging developments, including improvements at its Singapore operations and progress at its US gaming properties.

However, it cautioned that the group’s longer-term financial recovery would depend on its ability to translate heavy capital expenditure into stronger earnings and cash flow.

Persistent weakness at Genting Singapore, slower-than-expected earnings recovery in Las Vegas and New York, and additional debt-funded acquisitions remain key risks.

Overall, CreditSights viewed the RM1.25 billion rights issue as a positive development for Genting’s credit profile, but stressed that further deleveraging measures would be necessary to reduce downgrade risks and strengthen the group’s financial flexibility.

title: Genting loses RM1.6bil in market value after cash call
author: GURMEET KAUR
body:
PETALING JAYA: Genting Bhd shares plunged to a near two-decade low as investors balked at its proposed RM1.25bil rights issue, with concerns mounting over potential earnings dilution and whether the fundraising would do enough to ease the group’s hefty debt burden.
The sell-off prompted Bursa Malaysia to suspend intraday short selling (IDSS) in the stock for the rest of the day after its price fell beyond the prescribed threshold of 15% or 15 sen from its reference price.
IDSS is scheduled to resume today, the stock exchange operator said in a filing.
At market close, Genting shares fell 43 sen, or 22.87%, to RM1.45, wiping more than RM1.6bil off its market capitalisation.
At yesterday close, the stock’s market cap stood at RM5.58bil.
The selling pressure also spread to 73.8%-owned subsidiary, Genting Malaysia Bhd, whose shares fell 17.45%, or 26 sen, to RM1.23. IDSS in the counter was also suspended for the day.
A fund manager told StarBiz that Genting Bhd’s sharp share price decline was “largely expected” although the scale of the sell-off suggested growing investor concerns over the group’s balance sheet, potential earnings dilution and future funding needs amid significant capital commitments in Singapore and the United States.
He expects the near-term outlook to remain challenging over the next six to 12 months, with the rights issue coming at an uncomfortable time for shareholders.
“While the exercise may be financially prudent, the market is demanding greater discipline in capital management and clearer earnings visibility,” the fund manager said.
Last Friday, the gaming group announced a proposed renounceable rights issue to raise gross proceeds of RM1.25bil, with the issue price expected to be set at a 25% to 30% discount to the theoretical ex-rights price, based on the five-day volume-weighted average price before the price-fixing date.
The issue price, entitlement basis and final amount to be raised will be determined after shareholders’ approval is obtained at an EGM.
The proceeds will be used to repay RM800mil in borrowings maturing over the next 12 months, allocate RM429.5mil for general working capital and the balance to cover expenses related to the rights issue.
The group estimated that the reduced debt could save RM41.3mil of interest expenses annually (RM31.4mil post-tax), based on its weighted average interest rate of 5.16%.
The proposed exercise marks Genting’s first rights issue, coming as it reported a loss in the second quarter ended June 30 and carried borrowings of RM45.3bil as at end-June.
A head of research with a brokerage said the market is pricing in concerns of dilution, high leverage and future funding risks. He added that Genting’s challenge was not a lack of growth opportunities, but the funding required to realise them.
Improved cash flow could help ease the current pressure on its valuation, the research head said.
In a report, Maybank Investment Bank Research (Maybank IB) downgraded Genting to a “sell” from “buy” and cut its target price to RM1.49 from RM2.88, cautioning the rights issue could signal further equity fundraising or lower dividends.
“We note that Genting has been trying to refinance its borrowings to longer dated ones. This exercise concerns us because it signals to us that Genting probably has limited success in doing so,” the research firm said in an Oct 11 report.
Maybank IB said it does not rule out more equity fundraising efforts or fewer dividends as Genting rebuilds its cash balance.
Meanwhile, CIMB Research estimated that the exercise could dilute core earnings per share by 17% to 18% in the financial year 2027 (FY27) and FY28, based on an illustrative one-for-four entitlement priced at RM1.30 per share.
It said while the RM800mil debt repayment is expected to generate annual interest savings of RM41.3mil, net gearing would improve only modestly, from 102% to 94%, based on pro forma second-quarter FY26 figures.
Under this scenario, CIMB Research said it lowered its sum-of-parts target price to RM2.10 from RM2.30 previously.
It said investors generally view rights issues negatively because they replace debt with equity, which is a more expensive form of financing. However, it said the renounceable nature of the issue could help cushion some of the selling pressure.
PublicInvest Research viewed the rights issue as a more sensible funding avenue amid the group’s diminishing debt headroom and substantial capital commitments, particularly for Resorts World New York City in the United States and Resorts World Sentosa in Singapore.
The research house added that the recent rating downgrade by Fitch Ratings, and earlier cuts by Moody’s and S&P had increased its funding costs, thus making the cash call a more sensible way to raise funds amid potentially higher US dollar borrowing costs.
“The exercise allows Genting to raise utilisation of the proceeds up to 25% for the purposes it listed, which means that it could utilise up to RM1.1bil to repay debt without requiring additional shareholders’ approval by reducing the allocation for working capital or vice versa,” it added.
But given the uncertain earnings outlook, PublicInvest Research has maintained its “neutral” rating on the stock.
Last month, Fitch Ratings downgraded Genting and its subsidiary, Genting Malaysia, to BBB- from BBB, while maintaining a “stable” outlook for both.
The rating agency noted that Genting Malaysia’s New York casino expansion remained on track, although the substantial capital expenditure required would continue to put pressure on its credit metrics during the construction period.
Genting’s major shareholders, including Kien Huat Realty, Kien Huat International and Datuk Indera Lim Keong Hui, have irrevocably undertaken to subscribe for their full entitlements, collectively representing 45.1% of the proposed rights issue.
The remaining portion will be underwritten to ensure the issue is fully subscribed, the group had stated.
Genting is targeting completion of the rights issue in the first quarter of 2027.

title: Genting shares plunge as debt-reduction plan draws criticism
author: Focus Gaming News Editorial Team
body:
Genting shares plunge as debt-reduction plan draws criticism
The group plans to use US$195m to repay debt, but Maybank Investment Bank has downgraded its rating amid concerns over limited balance-sheet relief.
Key takeaways:
- Genting Berhad has proposed a MYR1.25bn (US$306m) rights issue to reduce debt and fund working capital. The company plans to allocate MYR800m (US$195m), or 64 per cent of the proceeds, to debt repayment over the next 12 months.
- Genting shares fell by over 22 per cent to MYR1.45 in trading today.
- Maybank Investment Bank downgraded Genting from Buy to Sell, citing limited balance-sheet relief and shareholder dilution.
Malaysia.- Genting Berhad’s proposed MYR1.25bn (US$306m) rights issue has sent its shares down by over 22 per cent today. The stock price fell to MYR1.45 as investors assess whether the capital raise will provide sufficient relief from the group’s debt burden.
Under the plan announced in a filing to Bursa Malaysia, Genting will allocate MYR800m (US$195m), 64 per cent of the proceeds, to pay down existing debt over the next 12 months, which the company estimates will generate MYR41.3m (US$10.1m) in annual interest savings. Another RM429.5m(US$105m) will support general working capital, with the remainder covering transaction costs.
Financial institutions responded cautiously to the announcement, questioning whether the planned debt repayment offers sufficient financial relief given the group’s total borrowings of MYR45.25bn ($11.07bn), which includes MYR9.68bn (US$2.63bn) in short-term debt due within the year. Maybank Investment Bank downgraded its rating on Genting from “Buy” to “Sell,” warning that the move provides only marginal relief to the group’s balance sheet while diluting shareholder value.
The capital raise highlights the growing financial pressure on Genting as it balances heavy capital expenditure against a large debt load. Major expansion commitments, including ongoing investments at Resorts World Sentosa in Singapore and the development of Resorts World New York City, have drawn recent scrutiny from rating agencies. Both Fitch Ratings and S&P Global Ratings previously cautioned that elevated spending and mixed operating results leave the group with minimal buffer to maintain its investment-grade status.
While key shareholders and major entities have committed to subscribe to 45.1 per cent of the target proceeds (MYR563.8m/ US$138m), the plan remains subject to shareholder approval at an extraordinary general meeting and regulatory approval from Bursa Malaysia. Genting targets completion of the rights issue by the first quarter of 2027.
Frequently asked questions (FAQs)
- Why is Genting launching a rights issue? Genting plans to use the proceeds primarily to reduce debt, with MYR800m earmarked for repayments over the next 12 months. The company expects this allocation to generate MYR41.3m in annual interest savings.
- Why did Genting shares fall today? Genting shares fell by over 22 per cent to MYR1.45 in trading today due to concerns that a proposed MYR1.25bn rights issue would provide only limited financial relief while diluting existing share value.
- How much debt does Genting have? Genting reported total borrowings of MYR45.25bn (US$11.07bn), including MYR9.68bn in short-term debt due within the year..

title: Genting Malaysia, Alibaba Cloud explore AI collaboration
author: Business Times
body:
KUALA LUMPUR: Genting Malaysia Bhd and Alibaba Cloud (Malaysia) Sdn Bhd have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to explore using artificial intelligence (AI) and cloud computing across the former's operations.
The agreement provides a framework for both parties to assess potential applications in employee productivity, operational efficiency and guest experience.
No specific projects or implementation timelines were disclosed.
Genting Malaysia deputy chief executive and executive director Datuk Indera Lim Keong Hui said the agreement will allow the group to evaluate potential applications before considering wider adoption.
"As a business with diverse operations, we see opportunities to evaluate how AI and cloud technologies can help our teams work more effectively and enhance the experiences we offer our guests," he said.
The MoU builds on an earlier collaboration involving Genting SkyWorlds Theme Park, where both parties explored the use of AI and cloud technology to support guest experience.
Alibaba Cloud Malaysia general manager Choong Hon Keat said the companies would assess further applications across Genting Malaysia's business functions, building on the earlier collaboration.
The agreement was signed at Alibaba Group's headquarters in Hangzhou, China.
The latest agreement does not commit either party to a specific deployment.
Both companies will assess potential use cases and their suitability for Genting Malaysia's operations before deciding whether to proceed with wider implementation.

title: Genting share price decline prompts IDSS suspension
author: The Star
body:

title: Genting Shares Plunge 22% As RM1.25 Billion Rights Issue Sparks Selling Pressure
body:
Genting Bhd shares plunged as much as 22% to RM1.45 on Monday (Oct 12), amid investor concerns over the group’s proposed RM1.25 billion rights issue, which could significantly dilute earnings per share (EPS) over the next two financial years.

The gaming and hospitality conglomerate closed on Froday at RM1.88 before falling to RM1.45 today during the trading session, reflecting selling pressure following the announcement of its fundraising exercise.

According to CIMB Securities, the proposed rights issue could dilute Genting’s core EPS by between 17% and 18% for financial years 2027 and 2028, although the exercise would help reduce debt and strengthen the group’s working capital position.

The research house had cautioned that the announcement could trigger a negative share price reaction as investors assessed the potential earnings dilution against the relatively modest improvement in the group’s financial gearing.

Genting plans to raise RM1.25 billion through a renounceable rights issue, with the shares expected to be priced at a 25% to 30% discount to the theoretical ex-rights price (TERP).

The fundraising exercise is expected to be completed in the first quarter of 2027.

Of the proceeds, RM800 million will be allocated towards repaying maturing debts, RM429.5 million for general working capital and RM20.5 million for expenses related to the exercise.

CIMB Securities estimated that the RM800 million debt repayment could generate annual interest savings of RM41.3 million, equivalent to RM31.4 million after tax.

However, the group’s pro forma net gearing would only decline to 94% from 102%, suggesting a relatively limited improvement in its balance sheet.

Under an illustrative scenario involving the issuance of approximately 962.6 million new shares at RM1.30 apiece, CIMB Securities estimated that Genting’s core EPS could be diluted by up to 18%.

The research house said the scenario would reduce its sum-of-parts-based target price to RM2.10, although it has maintained its existing valuation pending confirmation of the rights issue’s final terms.

CIMB Securities also noted that the renounceable structure would allow shareholders to sell their rights rather than subscribe for additional shares, potentially moderating selling pressure.

Nevertheless, the proposed fundraising exercise has raised concerns over shareholder dilution and the group’s ability to improve its financial position amid continued challenges facing its gaming and hospitality businesses.

title: Genting's RM1.25bil rights issue to cut debt, but earnings dilution looms
author: Nabiha Safian
body:
KUALA LUMPUR: Genting Bhd's proposed RM1.25 billion rights issue is expected to lower debt and financing costs, but potential earnings dilution and an uncertain operating outlook remain key concerns, said Public Investment Bank Bhd (PublicInvest).
PublicInvest said RM800 million, or 64 per cent of the proceeds, would be used to repay debt, while RM429.5 million, or 34.4 per cent, would fund working capital. The remaining RM20.5 million would cover expenses related to the rights issue, which is targeted for completion by the first quarter of financial year 2027 (1QFY27).
Genting's major shareholders, who collectively hold a 45.1 per cent stake, are expected to subscribe to their entitlements in full.
"Genting is expected to achieve potential interest savings of RM41.3 million per year following the repayment. The rights shares will be issued at a 25 per cent to 30 per cent discount to its five-day volume-weighted average price preceding the price-fixing date, while the entitlement ratio has yet to be determined," it said in a research note.
PublicInvest maintained its "Neutral" rating on Genting, citing limited earnings visibility, while setting a target price of RM2 after applying a 15 per cent holding company discount.
Based on an illustrative issue price of RM1.30 per share and an entitlement ratio of one rights share for every four existing shares, PublicInvest estimated that the exercise would dilute earnings per share (EPS).
The research house said the interest savings could lift Genting's earnings by 5.4 per cent and 4.2 per cent for FY27 and FY28, respectively.
However, the rights issue could dilute EPS by an estimated 16 per cent and 17 per cent for FY27 and FY28, respectively.
Dividends per share could also decline by about 20 per cent, while the group's gearing ratio is expected to ease marginally to 0.46 times from 0.47 times.
PublicInvest viewed the rights issue as a more sensible funding avenue amid diminishing debt headroom and rising financing costs.
It said Genting's substantial capital commitments, particularly for Resorts World New York City in the US and Resorts World Sentosa in Singapore, would require additional funding.
"We also believe that the recent downgrade by Fitch Ratings in September and earlier cuts by Moody's and S&P Global Ratings had increased its funding costs, thus making the cash call a more sensible way to raise funds," it said.
Higher US dollar financing costs could add further pressure, making the rights issue a more cost-effective alternative to raising additional debt.
Genting can vary the allocation of proceeds between debt repayment and working capital by up to 25 per cent for the stated purposes without seeking additional shareholder approval.
This flexibility could allow the group to allocate up to RM1.1 billion towards debt repayment by reducing the amount earmarked for working capital, or vice versa.
PublicInvest said prolonged geopolitical tensions, slowing economic activity and inflationary pressures could weigh on the global hospitality and entertainment industries.
Operating costs are also expected to rise in the second half of 2026, reflecting the secondary effects of higher energy prices.
"We do not expect the US operations to deliver higher earnings in the immediate term, in view of the weakening job market and consumer confidence.
"Among the business segments, Genting Plantations Bhd might be the bright spot due to strong crude palm oil prices, thus creating a buffer for the broader group," it said.
